title: Salman the Persian
hook: who left his fire-temple home searching, served Christian teachers, was enslaved, and found the Prophet ﷺ in Medina

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal, the muezzin, and a small prayer after wudu that was heard in the garden. Your line was the footsteps of bilal. What quiet habit did you keep? Day eight hundred twenty-four.

A young man in Persia has one job: keep the fire burning. His father, a landowner, loves him so much he barely lets him out of the house, and the household fire, the one his people tend in worship, must never go out. One day the father sends him to the fields. On the way he passes a church, hears people praying inside, and walks in. He stays until sunset. He never reaches the fields. That afternoon starts a long journey. Today: Salman the Persian, who tells his own story.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WHO KEEPS THE FIRE.` → `HE HEARS PRAYER IN A CHURCH.` → `HE NEVER REACHES THE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: The account comes in Salman's own voice, in the Musnad of Ahmad and in Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet. He leaves home for Syria, and attaches himself to Christian teachers, one after another, serving each until he dies. When the last of them is dying, Salman asks: who now? The old man tells him that a prophet will appear in the land of the Arabs, in a place of palm trees between two fields of black stone, and gives him signs to look for. So he sets out with traders, and they betray him and sell him as a slave. He's sold again, to a man in a town of palm trees. Medina. He's been carried, as a slave, to the place he was looking for. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, arrives there, Salman goes to him and watches, testing the signs one by one, and becomes a Muslim. The companions help him buy his freedom. Later, Bukhari tells of a day when the Prophet recited a verse about believers yet to come. In Pickthall's translation: "Along with others of them who have not yet joined them." Someone asked who those were. The Prophet put his hand on Salman and said that if faith were as far away as the Pleiades, men from among these people would reach it. Salman's story isn't a straight line. Fire, then church, then slavery, then Medina. Muslims remember him as a seeker, and every stage of the search counts in his telling: the home he left, the teachers who guided him, even the long wrong-way road that brought him to the right town.
screen: `FROM THE FIRE TO SYRIA.` · `TEACHER AFTER TEACHER.` · `SOLD, AND CARRIED TO MEDINA.` · `FAITH AT THE PLEIADES.` · then, large: `THE SEEKER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep searching. Sit, and breathe. Bring up one question about faith, or meaning, or how to live, that you haven't settled. Don't answer it. Just hold it, the way Salman held the old teacher's signs on the road. Then look back. Who has helped you with it so far? A book, a parent, a friend, a stranger? Let each one come with thanks. If you pray, you can ask God to guide you. If not, just let the question stay open, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Salman, the seeker who left the fire of his home, served Christian teachers, was sold as a slave, and found the Prophet in Medina. Today's word.
Your line: the seeker. Today, take one honest question a step further: read a page, ask someone wiser, or write it down where you'll see it. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Salman al-Farisi as a companion of the Prophet, retell his search as a story of seeking, and remember him in the account of the trench at Medina.

original.note: Arabic: Salman the Persian; al-Farisi means from Persia (Fars).

trapdoor: what you thought: a Persian man who became Muslim.
what it means: a seeker whose road ran from the fire of his home, through Christian teachers and slavery, to Medina.
what a scholar hears: the long account is in Salman's own voice in Ahmad's Musnad and Ibn Ishaq; Bukhari's report on 62:3 links him to believers yet to come.

notes: Ahmad 23737 numbering and the summary of Salman's account (father a landowner, keeping the fire, the church, teachers in Syria and beyond, the signs, betrayal by traders, sale in Medina): confirm. The account's numbers (teachers, palm trees, gold) are left out under the claims rule.
The account's episode of a corrupt bishop is deliberately omitted so that no tradition is made a foil; the Christian teachers are described respectfully.
Bukhari 4897 numbering and paraphrase (some versions: men, or a man, from these people): confirm.
Zoroastrian worship described only as tending the household fire 'in worship'; confirm the phrasing is respectful and accurate.
Editor: 'in chains' (not in the account) changed to 'as a slave'.

Audit: the teach claimed 'the story treats every stage with respect', which the full account does not (it includes the corrupt bishop this script omits); recast so the narrator makes no claim about the whole account.
